title: Ice Cream 1.5L

drivers.name: Price increase (2.3%) without promotion
drivers.evidence: At $6.56 (same price), sales were 24 (down 46% vs baseline) and 53 (up 19%). The dip was likely supply-related; the 53-unit week (up 19%) is more typical. However, no promotion or event that week. A 2.3% price hike with no offsetting driver likely reduces demand. Past price increases (no promotion)

adjustment.analysis: Baseline median is 44.3. No events in target week. Price is up 2.3% to $6.56 (vs. $6.41). Past price hikes show negative impact: at $6.56, sales were 24 units (2026-09-28) and 53 (2026-10-05), both below baseline. The 2026-09-28 spike to 24 units was likely a stockout or supply issue (no event noted). The 2026-10-05 week at $6.56 sold 53 units, 19% above baseline. But this was not a promotion. A 2.3% price increase with no promotion is likely to dampen demand. Past price increases (e.g., 2026-09-28) show demand drop. No promotion or event to offset. Adjust down. Noise-adjusted evidence is thin (one past price increase at same level). Shrink toward 1.0.

brief:
PRODUCT: Ice Cream 1.5L | category Frozen | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-16 to 2026-11-22 (6 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 6.56 (+2.3% vs regular price 6.41)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 44.3 | 5%-95%: 13.0 - 73.8 | 10%-90%: 21.3 - 69.6

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-36% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
